quote: each Party shall have the right to exploit, including license, the Joint Program Technology, without a duty of accounting or any obligation to seek consent from the other Party to exploit such Joint Program Technology. To the extent necessary to effect the foregoing in a country other than the United States, each Party grants to the other Party a nonexclusive, irrevocable, perpetual, fully-paid, worldwide license, with the right to grant sublicenses, under the granting Party's interest in Joint Program Technology, for any and all purposes
rationale: The IP architecture protects Sanofi and creates no prohibited transfer to RevMed. Section 10.1(a) requires each Party to obtain assignment of Program Inventions from its own Third Parties to that Party (and Section 3.4 requires subcontractor assignment, or failing that an irrevocable, perpetual, fully-paid, exclusive, royalty-free worldwide licence with sublicensing rights to the engaging Party), so work generated for Sanofi vests in Sanofi; "Sanofi Sole Program Know-How"/"Sanofi Sole Program Patents" (1.109-1.110) confirm Sanofi solely owns its own Program Inventions and Section 10.4(c) gives Sanofi sole enforcement of them. Joint Program Technology is jointly owned but each Party may exploit and license it with no duty of accounting and no consent, backed by a perpetual, irrevocable, fully-paid, worldwide, sublicensable cross-licence — i.e. joint ownership with an unrestricted right to exploit, which sits at the fallback rather than the "no joint ownership" preferred position and is therefore acceptable. Sanofi's data and regulatory position are preserved and enhanced: RevMed assigns all Regulatory Approvals (INDs/NDAs) to Sanofi (6.2), transfers the global safety database at its own cost (6.5), and Sanofi owns all Product Marks and domain names (10.5). There is no assignment of Sanofi background IP or Sanofi Sole Program Technology to RevMed: Section 3.2 is only a narrow non-exclusive, royalty-free sublicence back of RevMed's own licensed technology solely to let RevMed perform its obligations, and Section 3.6 negates implied licences. The Article XII reversion is a bargained-for, licence-based unwind limited to Termination Products, triggered largely by Sanofi's own convenience/change-of-control election or Sanofi default, and carries post-termination royalties payable to Sanofi (12.3(c)(ii)C). Noted but not flagged: the ownership allocation in 10.1(a) is redacted [***], so the sole/joint split is inferred from the defined terms; if the unredacted text allocated Sanofi-generated inventions to RevMed we would revisit.

quote: 14.5 Limitation of Liability. NEITHER PARTY SHALL BE LIABLE TO THE OTHER FOR ANY SPECIAL, CONSEQUENTIAL, INCIDENTAL, PUNITIVE, OR INDIRECT DAMAGES OR LOST PROFITS ARISING FROM OR RELATING TO ANY BREACH OF THIS AGREEMENT, REGARDLESS OF ANY NOTICE OF THE POSSIBILITY OF SUCH DAMAGES.
rationale: Section 14.5 is the only limitation-of-liability provision in the Agreement (searches for "aggregate liability" and other cap language return nothing else, and Section 14.6 expressly says insurance does not create a liability limit). It is mutual and waives indirect/consequential damages and lost profits, and it preserves the indemnities under Sections 14.1-14.2, confidentiality (Article XI) and IP (Article X) outside that waiver — all consistent with the playbook's carve-out expectations. However, there is no monetary cap of any kind: both Parties' direct-damages exposure is unlimited. That fails the fallback, which requires a mutual cap of at least twelve months' fees. As the paying party facing uncapped direct-damages claims (for example for alleged breach of diligence or of Article XIV obligations), a mutual cap is materially in our interest. Redline inserts a mutual cap at the greater of twelve months' payments and USD 1,000,000, keeps the existing indemnity/confidentiality/IP carve-outs plus gross negligence, willful misconduct and fraud outside the cap, and confirms Sanofi's payment obligations are not "damages" for cap purposes.

Sanofi therefore has no obligation to extend RevMed terms no less favourable than those given to any third party or to match third-party offers, which meets the preferred position (no MFN obligation on Customer). No redline is warranted; a Vendor-granted MFN would also be acceptable but none exists here.

quote: 13.5 No Other Warranties. EXCEPT AS EXPRESSLY STATED IN THIS ARTICLE XIII, (A) NO REPRESENTATION, CONDITION OR WARRANTY WHATSOEVER IS MADE OR GIVEN BY OR ON BEHALF OF SANOFI OR REVMED; AND (B) ALL OTHER CONDITIONS AND WARRANTIES WHETHER WRITTEN OR ORAL OR EXPRESS OR IMPLIED ARE HEREBY EXPRESSLY EXCLUDED, INCLUDING ANY CONDITIONS AND WARRANTIES OF MERCHANTABILITY, FITNESS FOR A PARTICULAR PURPOSE OR NON-INFRINGEMENT.
rationale:
This is a drug research/development and commercialization collaboration, not a services or software purchase, so the rule's parameters map onto RevMed's performance standards and warranty package rather than a fixed software/deliverable conformance period. The material protections the rule targets are all present and sit at or above the fallback:

1. Performance standard (the "professional and workmanlike" analogue): Section 4.2(b) (p0291) and Section 5.2(b) (p0313) require RevMed to perform all Research and Development activities "in compliance with all Applicable Law (including GMP, GLP and GCP)" and to use diligent efforts to conduct activities in accordance with each Research/Development Plan, including timelines. GMP/GLP/GCP is the industry-standard equivalent of the preferred workmanlike/industry-standards covenant.

2. Real remedy: Sections 4.2(b) and 5.2(b) give a graduated cure mechanic (JRDC/JSC-specified cure actions, cure periods) followed by Sanofi step-in/transfer rights "without prejudice to any other rights or remedies Sanofi may have under this Agreement or otherwise at law or in equity" (p0292, p0314). Re-performance and cure are therefore backed by full retained remedies, plus RevMed indemnifies Sanofi for material breach of its warranties (p0583) and material breach supports termination. This is a stronger remedy than the rule's repair/replace/refund floor.

3. Compliance with laws: warranted at Section 13.2(u) (p0564) and covenanted mutually at Section 13.4(b) (p0572).

4. Express warranty not swallowed by the disclaimer: Section 13.5 opens with "EXCEPT AS EXPRESSLY STATED IN THIS ARTICLE XIII," which preserves the entire Article XIII package — RevMed's twenty-one express representations and warranties in Section 13.2 (p0543 et seq.) covering sole ownership free of liens, no prior encumbrance, right to grant the licenses, non-infringement, non-misappropriation, patent validity and enforceability, no litigation, no government-funding encumbrance, and completeness of diligence disclosures. This is the opposite of the walk-away "AS IS with all warranties disclaimed" position.

5. Product conformance: Section 7.3 (p0360) defers conformance to a negotiated Supply Agreement and Quality Agreement, which "shall cover the documentation and other quality requirements for the acceptance of previously manufactured supply of Product" — the correct home for batch-level conformance and acceptance/rejection remedies in a pharma collaboration.

Sub-elements short of the preferred wording, noted rather than flagged: there is no fixed-duration (12-month/90-day) conformance-to-documentation warranty with an express repair/replace/refund election, and no "no malicious code" warranty — neither maps to this deal type, as there is no software or discrete deliverable, and product conformance is expressly routed to the Supply and Quality Agreements. Two minor points to track rather than redline here: (a) the Section 13.2 warranties are given only "as of the Execution Date," which is standard for a transaction of this type and is supplemented by the forward-looking covenants in Sections 13.3 and 13.4; and (b) when negotiating the Supply and Quality Agreements under Section 7.3 we should secure an express batch conformance warranty (GMP, specifications, no adulteration) with replacement-or-refund remedies, and confirm Section 13.5 is not read to reach warranties given in those Ancillary Agreements.

No redline proposed — the clause meets the fallback on its material terms and the disclaimer benefits from a proper carve-out, so flagging would be counterproductive.

quote: 14.6 Insurance. Each Party shall procure and maintain insurance, including product liability insurance, with respect to its activities hereunder and under the Ancillary Agreements and which is consistent with normal business practices of companies similarly situated at all times during which any SHP2 Inhibitors or Product is being clinically tested in human subjects or commercially distributed or sold. Sanofi may fulfill such obligation through self- insurance. Each Party shall provide the other Party with evidence of such insurance upon request
rationale: An insurance clause is present (Section 14.6), so the rule's "missing" trigger is not met. RevMed is bound to procure and maintain insurance — expressly including product liability cover, the line most relevant to a clinical/commercial collaboration of this kind — at levels consistent with normal business practices of similarly situated companies, for the whole period during which SHP2 Inhibitors or Product are in human clinical testing or commercial distribution. The clause also delivers the two mechanics the playbook cares about beyond limits: evidence of insurance on request, and (one-way in our favour) advance written notice from RevMed of cancellation, non-renewal or material change. It further confirms that insurance does not cap either Party's Article XIV indemnification obligations, preserving our recovery against RevMed. Several terms run in our favour and should not be flagged: the obligation is mutual, and Sanofi alone may satisfy it through self-insurance. On its material terms this sits at the fallback rather than the preferred position. Noted but not flagged: there are no stated dollar limits (no CGL 1M/2M, no E&O, no cyber/privacy tower) and no one-year tail after the term. Those preferred-position specifics are of limited weight here because RevMed is a licensor/co-development counterparty rather than a hosting or data-processing vendor — it does not host our systems or work on our premises, so the walk-away scenario (no insurance for a vendor processing personal data or working on-site) is not engaged. Per the playbook's classification semantics, these are sub-elements short of preferred wording and are recorded in the rationale rather than redlined.

verification.notes: The rule is a 'missing'-kind insurance check, and Section 14.6 is a genuine, mutual insurance covenant (including product liability) running through clinical testing and commercialization, so the missing/insert trigger is not engaged and the deterministic check confirms an insurance obligation is present. The rationale accurately reflects the quoted text: evidence of insurance on request, one-way advance notice from RevMed of cancellation/non-renewal/material change, self-insurance permitted only for Sanofi (our side), and an express statement that insurance does not cap Article XIV indemnification — all neutral or favourable to us, so no redline is warranted. Shortfalls versus the preferred position (no CGL 1M/2M, no E&O or cyber towers, no one-year tail) are correctly recorded in the rationale rather than redlined; the walk-away scenario (no insurance for a data-processing or on-site vendor) is not engaged for a licensor/co-development counterparty, and the rule is low severity. Consistent with the claimed compliant status, no redline text was changed and no counterparty comment was proposed, so there is no risk of over-flagging or an invalid edit. Minor: describing a limits-free 'normal business practices' standard as sitting squarely 'at the fallback' (E&O USD 1M / cyber USD 2M) is generous phrasing, but the rationale discloses the absence of stated limits, so the classification remains defensible and non-actionable.
